Response to the Reviewer 1:
Thank you so much for your careful review and constructive suggestions! Based on your
suggestions, we have made substantial improvements and updated our manuscript
accordingly, with all changes highlighted in yellow. Here, we provide our responses to each
of your points. For your convenience, we first state your comments in italic and then
provide our responses.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript by Yijun Fan et al. presents an exome-wide association study assessing
rare coding variants associated with 596 multi-organ MRI traits in over 50,000 individuals
from the UK Biobank. The study uses both variant-level and gene-based burden
associations to explore how these variants contribute to the structure and function of
human organs. While the analysis is extensive and well-documented, I have concerns
regarding the reliability of the novel loci identified.
Response: Thank you very much for reviewing our paper and your constructive comments!
We appreciate that you have highlighted the strengths of our study, including the extensive
analysis across muti-organ MRI traits, both variant-level and gene-based analyses, and the
well-documented steps. Following your comments, we conducted additional analyses and
provided clarifications to improve the reliability of the newly identified loci. We have tried
our best to improve this work by closely following your specific questions and suggestions
below.
Major comments:
1. The authors have chosen joint analysis and internal replication to validate their findings.
Given that meta-analysis is a robust method for integrating results across multiple GWAS
to identify novel loci, could the authors clarify why this approach was not considered?
Response: Thank you so much for your insightful question! We agree that meta-analysis is a
robust and convenient method for integrating results across multiple studies with only
summary statistics is available, especially for common variant analysis in GWAS. In this UK
Biobank-based WES study, we had full access to individual-level data from 54,365 European
participants, enabling us to directly perform a joint analysis on the pooled sample to
estimate summary statistics. Therefore, we first reported the association analysis based on
the joint sample, which maximizes statistical power by leveraging all available data. To make
the best use of this data resource for evaluating reproducibility, we further split the sample
into independent internal discovery and validation subsets for an internal replication
analysis. This line of reasoning led us to favor a joint analysis over a meta-analysis in our
study design.
some variants (for example, with frequencies as low as MAF < 1 × 10⁻⁴) poses unique
challenges, making meta-analysis particularly challenging. For example, in gene-based
burden tests, rare variants are aggregated within a gene based on functional annotation and
MAF thresholds. However, given a specific gene region and a predefined burden mask, the
sets of variants identified in the discovery and validation samples may differ, making the
results not fully comparable and complicating gene-level meta-analysis of rare variants.
Based on these considerations, using a joint analysis for the primary results, alongside an
internal replication strategy via sample splitting, was motivated by several factors. First,
given the low MAF of rare mutations, joint analysis enhances the stability of summary
statistics and may increase statistical power. Second, this design allows us to make full use
of the available data to evaluate the robustness of associations identified through both
variant-level and gene-level tests in a conventional manner for validation analysis.
Furthermore, in the absence of non-UK Biobank WES datasets of comparable size suitable
for replicating associations with complex imaging phenotypes, our approach also provides
broader insights into the replicability of such phenotypes, for example, by quantifying the
proportion of signals that can be confirmed given the available sample size.
As noted by Reviewer 2, the lack of external validation datasets is a common limitation in
current WES analyses. When additional external data sources become available, it will be
highly valuable to conduct similar rare variant association studies for imaging traits, as done
in our UK Biobank study. Meta-analysis using summary statistics from multiple studies can
then be performed to integrate and better validate the findings. Following your comments,
we have clarified the considerations that we adopted this internal discovery-replication
design within the UK Biobank study and mentioned the benefits of meta-analysis in the
future studies to integrate results from multiple studies. In the revised manuscript, we have
included these details in main text, discussion, and Supplementary Note:
“Specifically, all the primary findings and the corresponding interpretations are based on the
joint sample for higher statistical power and more stable summary statistics. Then the joint
sample was split into the internal discovery sample and validation sample to verify the
robustness of the findings within the UKB study (Fig. 1, Methods, and Supplementary
Note).” (Page 5, Lines 2-6)
“Consequently, this led us to use joint analysis with a stringent P-value cutoff, and an
internal validation procedure to assess the robustness of our findings” (Page 25, Lines 20-22)
“When future data resources become available, it will be valuable to replicate our findings
and extend the scope of WES studies across multiple cohorts. Meta-analysis may be a robust
and efficient approach for identifying and replicating associations using only summary
statistics.” (Page 25, Lines 28-31)
2. In Page 5, Line 18, the manuscript states that 107 rare variant-level associations were
identified using a conservative P-value threshold. However, the derivation of these 107
associations from the reported 59 that passed the Bonferroni threshold is unclear.
Furthermore, it is mentioned that 48 of these 59 associations had mutations with a Minor
Allele Count (MAC) > 5. It seems there might be a discrepancy in the numbers reported or a
potential misunderstanding in how these figures relate. Could the authors clarify how the
total of 107 was reached and confirm whether all these associations also underwent
internal replication and joint analysis?
Response: Thank you so much for pointing this out! We appreciate your careful review on
the details of our association results. The “107 rare variant-level associations” were
identified based on the joint sample (phase 1 to phase 5) with a stringent P-value cutoff at
2.8 × 10-10. The “59 associations” were identified using the internal discovery sample (phase
1 to phase 3, a subset of the joint sample) specifically for the internal replication analysis.
That is, all 107 associations were identified through the joint analysis, leveraging the full
sample size to maximize discovery power. However, for the internal replication analysis, we
split the data, and only 59 associations derived from a subset of the sample were evaluated.
Specifically, we first conducted the joint analysis to report the 107 significant associations
and then split the joint sample into the internal discovery sample and validation sample as
mentioned in our manuscript and the response to your Comment 1. The P-value cutoff for
the discovery sample was achieved by the same procedure as the joint sample, resulting in
59 significant variant-level associations. For these 59 associations, we found that 48 of them
have MAC > 5 in the validation sample (phase 4 to phase 5) and were suitable for
association testing. During this revision, we have provided additional information, such as
the MAC for all identified rare variants in the validation sample, which may be helpful for
clarification.
Following your suggestions, we have carefully reviewed the results and added additional
columns to Table S4 for the variant-level tests in the validation sample, including MAC
values and indicators for the variants excluded from the validation tests as well as for
whether the variants passed the internal replication steps. In the revised manuscript, we
have also clarified procedures for the variant-level tests and explicitly stated the number of
discoveries and their relationships. These clarifications are included in the main text,
Supplementary Note, and the updated Table S4 to avoid any potential misunderstandings:
“To assess the reliability of our findings derived from the joint sample and make full use of
available data, we adopted an internal replication procedure30. (Fig. 1, Methods, and
Supplementary Note). Specifically, we split the joint sample to the internal discovery dataset
and validation dataset after joint analysis for internal replication. The discovery dataset
included individuals from phases 1 to 3 of MRI release (average n = 30,739) and is a subset of
the joint sample, while the validation dataset is independent of it by design and contained
individuals from phases 4 to 5 of the MRI release (Method, average n = 8,989). For the
purpose of replication analysis, summary statistics from the discovery sample will be
separately compared with results from the validation sample and the joint sample (Method
and Supplementary Note). When we restricted our study to the discovery sample, 59
associations passed the Bonferroni threshold of P < 3.5 × 10-10 ... and were used for internal
replication.” (Page 6, Lines 6-18)
“...48 had mutations with MAC > 5 suitable for association tests (Table S4) in the
independent validation sample…” (Page 6, Lines 18-20)
3
“Consequently, this led us to use joint analysis with a stringent P-value cutoff, and an
internal validation procedure to assess the robustness of our findings” (Page 25, Lines 20-22)
3. For a clearer understanding of the impact and reliability of the reported associations,
please provide detailed statistical information (such as Beta, P-values) for the 107 rare
variant-level associations across different phases (1-3, 4-5) and in the joint analysis.
Response: Thank you so much for your suggestions! Following your comment (including
previous ones), we have provided a clearer summary of our study design and the details of
association tests conducted across different phases.
Specifically, as explained in our main text and the responses to your previous comments, the
107 associations identified in the joint sample are our primary findings and all the summary
statistics can be found in Table S2. They include both the associations restricted to the
discovery sample and associations unique to the joint sample.
When restricted to the discovery sample, 59 associations were identified for replication
analysis. The summary statistics (including Beta and P-values) for these 59 associations from
the internal discovery sample, those available in validation sample, and those available in
the joint sample have already been provided in Table S4. Following your suggestions, we
added several additional columns including MAC, number of individuals, indicator of the
results for clearer understanding of the impact and reliability of the associations and
statistical information. We also explicitly pointed out these details in the main text:
“More details of the results from the internal replication analysis and summary statistics of
variant-level associations across different stages can be found in Table S4.” (Page 7, Lines 4-
6)
4. Similar to the variant-level associations, the details surrounding the 244 gene-based
associations are not entirely clear. Including a detailed workflow, possibly in the
supplementary materials, might help clarify the process by which these associations were
identified and analyzed.
Response: Thank you so much for your suggestions! Similar to variant-level tests, these 224
gene-based associations were based on the joint sample (phase 1 to phase 5) and they are
our primary findings. For internal replication, we only conducted the confirmation analysis
between the discovery sample (phase 1 to phase 3) and the joint sample as gene-based
testing based on validation sample is not comparable with the discovery sample or joint
sample due to the limited sample size mentioned in the main text and in the response to
your Comment 1. Following your comments, we have provided similar details and statistical
information in Table S9. We also clarified the process in the main text and in the
Supplementary Note:
“Therefore, we only made use of the internal discovery sample and examined..., similar to
internal-replication analysis for variant-level tests (Methods and Supplementary Note)”
(Page 11, Lines 18-21)
4
“The detailed summary statistics and results of internal replication analysis for gene-based
associations have been provided in Table S9.” (Page 11, Lines 25-27)
5. On Page 6, the comparison between effect directions and P-values is noted, but there is
no mention of comparing effect sizes. Did the authors evaluate the correlation of effect
sizes across studies? Including this analysis would provide deeper insights into the
consistency of the associations identified.
Response: Thank you so much for your insightful suggestion! Following your suggestion, we
have added the correlation metric in the validation stage for variant-level associations to
verify the consistency of the associations identified. We agree that the correlation of effect
sizes between discovery sample and validation sample is interpretable as they are from
independent samples.
Specifically, for all the variant-level associations identified in the phase 1 to phase 3
discovery sample under the primary p-value cutoff at 3.5 × 10-10 as well as a more
permissive cutoff at 1 × 10-8, we retrieved the effect sizes of 48 associations available in the
validation sample for the correlation test (with MAC > 5). Then, we conducted Pearson
correlation test for those associations with summary statistics available in both stages. The
correlation showed that the associations across the two stages are consistent. Specifically,
at the primary threshold 3.5 × 10-10, there are 48 (out of 59) associations with both stages of
summary statistics available, and we have observed great correlation of effect sizes (r =
g
0.935, P = 2.8 × 10-22). At a more lenient cutoff 1 × 10-8, there were 83 (out of 154)
associations available for both stages and showed moderate correlation (r = 0.653, P = 2.2 ×
g
10-11). Overall, the associations identified showed consistency across the discovery and
validation sample, while it also verified that our primary threshold gave a credible set of
associations. In this revision, we have added the results of correlation test in the main text:
“We conducted the Pearson correlation test for the effect sizes of the identified associations
in the discovery sample and the validation sample. Among these 48 associations with
summary statistics available in both stages, we observed a substantial correlation (r = 0.935,
g
P = 2.8 × 10-22), which shows a high level of agreement between the associations identified in
the discovery sample and validation sample. When we relaxed the P-value cutoff to 1 × 10-8,
there was still a moderate to high correlation (r = 0.653, P = 2.2 × 10-11).” (Page 6, Lines 23-
g
29)
6. Considering the manuscript addresses both variant-level and gene-based associations, it
would be beneficial to understand if there are overlapping signals between these two
levels of analysis. Such overlaps could signify particularly robust associations.
Response: Thank you so much for your insightful comments! We agree that evaluating
overlapping signals between variant-level and gene-based tests is interesting, as these tests
examine associations from different perspectives/assumptions and can yield
complementary insights. Therefore, the overlapping signals indicate that both a single rare
variant in this region and the joint effects of multiple variants across the region are both
strong enough to drive a significant association. In our study, we found that ANO1 with
5
max/min aorta area and TNFRSF13B with spleen volume are the associations shared in both
variant-level and gene-based signals. We discussed these associations respectively in our
original manuscript. In the revised manuscript, we highlighted these associations and
emphasized the fact that they are overlapping signals in the main text following your
suggestion:
“Three gene-trait pairs overlapped across variant-level and gene-level tests (two
associations between ANO1 and max/min aorta area, and an association between
TNFRSF13B and spleen volume), indicating that both a single rare variant in this region and
the joint effects of variants across the region are strong enough to drive an association.”
(Page 11, Lines 5-10)
Meanwhile, we would like to note that the WES literature generally expects variant-level
and gene-level tests to capture distinct signals (such as Wang et al., Nature PMID: 34375979;
Backman et al., Nature PMID: 34662886; Karczewski et al., Cell Genom. PMID: 36778668).
For example, gene-based burden test is more powerful for identifying signals driven by pLoF
variants as these variants are rare individually but have consistent effect directions
(Karczewski et al., Cell Genom. PMID: 36778668), while the pattern for missense variants in
variant-level tests and gene-level tests is less obvious (Backman et al., Nature PMID:
34662886; Karczewski et al., Cell Genom. PMID: 36778668). These observations are
consistent with our findings. In the revised manuscript, we have also discussed this point in
the discussion:
“Analyses at the variant level and gene-based burden level may yield complementary
insights into gene associations. For example, gene-based burden testing is more powerful for
identifying signals driven by pLoF variants as these variants are rare individually but have
consistent effect directions17, while the pattern for missense variants signals in variant-level
tests and gene-level tests is less obvious16,17,61. In our study, we found that pLoF signals were
exclusively detected by gene-based tests, whereas three gene–trait pairs were observed
across both variant- and gene-level analyses. This pattern aligns with previous findings and
underscores the importance of incorporating both approaches. Moreover, although gene-
based burden tests can enhance signal detection16,17, annotating the deleterious variants is
still an active research area.” (Page 23, Lines 6-15)
Minor comments:
1. The manuscript mentions that 8,127,841 variants remained after quality control for
downstream analyses (Page 38, Line 5). However, there seems to be a discrepancy, as

Can the authors clarify these numbers? Specifically, how do the 8,127,841 variants relate
to the much larger number used for the Bonferroni correction?
Response: Thank you so much for your careful review! The 8,127,841 was the number of
variants that were filtered after the basic quality control steps before functional annotation
(Page 41, Line 8). After annotation, only coding variants of interest were included in the
association tests (specifically predicted loss-of-function variants and missense variants,
6
defined in the annotation section in Methods). This step would further filter out a subset of
2,143,707 variants of interest for association tests (Page 41, Line 28).
The key reason we use a much larger number for the Bonferroni correction is that we
additionally adjust for all imaging phenotypes. Specifically, the Bonferroni correction was
adjusted for the number of all the variant-level tests conducted based on these coding
variants of interest across all the 596 phenotypes. This would give us a quite stringent
threshold to determine the significant variants. Additionally, REGENIE computed the MAC
for each phenotype, and following its suggested and default settings, only variants or gene
masks with MAC > 5 were used for association testing, as described in our original
manuscript. Thus, a great number of rare variants would be omitted due to insufficient MAC
and the number of tests omitted was reported in the log files for each phenotype category.
For example, in the variant-level tests of 101 brain volume phenotypes, 690,562,178 tests in
total were ignored due to low MAC as documented in the log files, which means 6,837,249
variants were ignored on average for each brain volume phenotype. Meanwhile, there were
130,349,763 results (including all the variants after quality control) observed in the variant-
level tests for these 101 brain volume phenotypes and we focused on 31,096,939 results
among them for coding variants of interest based on the annotation results. This means
1,290,592 variants (including both coding variants of interest and other variants) are present
for each brain volume phenotype and among them 307890.5 variants were coding variants
of interest on average. Finally, the number of all categories of variants present and the
number of variants ignored on average for each brain volume phenotype would add up to
the total number of variants after quality control, that is 8,127,841 (=1,290,592+6,837,249).
But we would like to emphasize that the number 31,096,939 would be used for multiple
testing adjustment for the part of 101 brain volume phenotypes (corresponding to 307890.5
on average for each of the brain volume phenotypes) as they represent the number of
coding variants.
Based on these facts, we manually retrieved the number of coding variants of interest
included in the variant-level tests for each of the 596 phenotypes by customized code for
precise multiple testing adjustment. Finally, the number of tests for each organ category of
phenotypes (such as 31,096,939 for brain volume phenotypes) was summed up and this
would yield 178,280,016 variant-trait tests in total as documented in Table S24. We also
included the total number of variant-level tests for each phenotype category in Table S24,
which is helpful to track the number of variants.
Following your question, we have carefully checked our procedure and put this example
into Supplementary Note for illustration. We have also clarified it in the revised manuscript
and Table S24:
“The variant-level tests include all the coding variants of interest (n = 2,143,707) across all
596 phenotypes, but only those with sufficient MAC (MAC > 5) were tested and the MAC was
calculated for each phenotype respectively by REGENIE, so a large number of tests of
variants with MAC < 5 were ignored (Supplementary Note). The summary count and more
details are available in Table S24.” (Page 43, Lines 11-16)
7
2. Please provide clearly variants number and/or gene number in each stage.
Response: Thank you so much for your suggestion! Following your suggestion, we added the
number of variants and genes for association tests in the joint sample. The validation
analysis was only performed for the identified associations from the discovery sample for
variant-level tests and was not conducted for gene-based burden tests. We also provided
the average number of variants tested in the internal discovery sample and joint sample, as
this would give a clearer intuition of the number of tests affected by the sample size. In the
revised manuscript, we have made such changes:
“The variant-level tests include all the coding variants of interest (n = 2,143,707) across all
596 phenotypes, but only those with sufficient MAC (MAC > 5) were tested and the MAC was
calculated for each phenotype respectively by REGENIE, so a large number of tests of
variants with MAC < 5 were ignored (Supplementary Note). The summary count and more
details are available in Table S24. Briefly, 2,143,707 coding variants of interest were included
for variant-level association tests, and an average of 299,128 tests were conducted for each
phenotype in joint sample and similarly an average of 239,825 tests per phenotype were
conducted for the discovery sample (Table S24 and Supplementary Note).” (Page 43, Lines
11-20)
“A total number of 17,474 genes are available for burden tests in the joint sample and
discovery sample. Using the same joint sample as in variant-level tests...” (Page 10, Lines 28-
31)
3. There are numerous NA entries in the BETAorg (95% CI) and Unit columns of Table 1.
Could the authors explain the reason for these missing values?
Response: Thank you very much for pointing this out! These NA entries in the BETAorg (95%
CI) and Unit columns of Table 1 correspond to DTI traits and fMRI traits. For DTI and fMRI
phenotypes, the physical unit is typically missing or not interpretable. Instead, these kinds of
phenotypes may stand for summary signals extracted from the measurements to indicate
some specific types of information. By contrary, structural traits are more interpretable in
terms of physical unit (for example, volume), so the original units would offer more intuitive
information regarding the effect sizes for these traits. For clarification, we have mentioned
it in the caption of Table 1 in the revised manuscript:
“Additional original units were provided for structural traits including regional brain volumes,
abdominal MRI traits, and CMR traits for intuitive interpretations of the effect sizes.” (The
caption of Table 1, Page 50, Lines 17-19)
Thank you so much for your careful review and constructive suggestions! Based on your
suggestions, we have made substantial improvements and updated our manuscript
accordingly, with all changes highlighted in yellow. Here, we provide our responses to each
of your points. For your convenience, we first state your comments in italic and then
provide our responses.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this work Fan et al. investigate the link between rare genetic variation measured using
exome sequence and MRI-derived phenotypes for 3 ‘organs’ (brain, heart, abdomen). They
filtered down from millions of rare variants by restricting the analysis to damaging
variants as predicted by various tools (classic ones as well as AlphaMissense). The analysis
is restricted to the UK Biobank. Since there were no external validation datasets (as is
common in genetics) the authors split the UK Biobank into a discovery and a validation
cohort. Imaging releases 1 to 3 were used for discovery and releases 4 to 5 were used for
validation. However, the nature of rare variants means that some identified SNPs were
not present in the validation dataset (with about 10k people in the validation you can
expect two carriers of the variant at MAF 0.0001). In such cases the authors considered a
confirmatory analysis if the direction was maintained and the p-value improved.
In addition to the variant-level analysis the authors conducted a series of gene-burden
tests using various groupings of the rare variants based on the algorithms that rated them
as damaging. These tests uncovered a few additional gene-trait associations that were not
picked up by single variant tests.
The authors then discuss some of the gene-trait associations grouped by organ and by
analysis technique. Focusing on three different organs renders these discussions quite long
and probably only interesting to researchers who are working on the specific organ. While
others might simply skip these parts. The synergy between organs appears to be limited.
There is a link between cardiac associations and fMRI-traits, which is sensible and has
been commented on before.
There are a few novel findings, some of them support gene-trait associations that have
been uncovered with GWAS in the same cohort. Overall, this is a large dataset and it is
somewhat surprising that not more associations were revealed by this analysis.
Overall, this manuscript is well written and easy to follow. The authors conducted a lot of
analyses (e.g., it is nice to evaluate the effects of different SNP annotations and the drug
target database enrichment). In my opinion the statistics are appropriate although there
remain some questions about the detailed methodology.
Response: Thank you very much for reviewing our paper and for your insightful comments!
We completely agree that including extensive analyses such as incorporating multiple
annotation strategies, conducting both variant-level and gene-level tests, and leveraging
9
other data sources such as drug target database could be interesting. We also appreciate
that you have highlighted our study design inspired by the limitations of rare variant
association studies. For example, the nature of rare mutation requires relatively large
sample to investigate, and the lack of external dataset poses a challenge on validation
analysis. We have tried our best to improve this work by carefully following your
constructive comments and questions below.
Major
1. It is unclear how the exome sequencing data was pre-processed. Presumably the
authors did not conduct the analysis from scratch and relied on the VCF files provided by
UK Biobank. However, it would still be great to provide a summary of the processing
details from raw sequences to called variants.
Response: Thank you so much for your suggestion! We have provided the relevant
information and citations (Hout et al. Nature, PMID: 33087929, Szustakowski et al. Nat
Genet. PMID: 34183854) about the pre-processing steps of exome sequencing data from UK
Biobank in the revised manuscript:
“Whole-exome sequencing (WES) data were obtained from the UK Biobank and the detailed
sequencing protocols can be found elsewhere18. By following a unified OQFE protocol121, raw
sequencing reads were aligned to the GRCh38 reference genome, and small variants were
called on a per-sample basis using DeepVariant. Per-sample gVCFs were then joint-
genotyped using GLnexus to produce multi-sample project-level VCFs (pVCF) suitable for
association analysis. We made use of the OQFE WES files in BGEN format provided by UK
Biobank after these centrally pre-processing steps.” (Page 39, Lines 16-22)
2. It is not very clear how exactly the authors arrive at the multiple testing threshold. Even
the Supplementary table 21 does not quite reveal the underlying principle sufficiently. It
does not even become clear whether the threshold is adjusted for all the different imaging
traits. For instance for the volume trait there are 101 phenotypes and 31096939
Variants tested. Does that mean that there are 307890.5 variants tested per phenotype? If
that is the case, then the authors should also emphasize that their adjustment is quite
stringent because the phenotypes are not independent. Please, can the authors clarify this
aspect of the analysis.
Response: Thank you so much for your careful review! The Bonferroni correction was
adjusted for all the variant-level tests conducted based on these coding variants of interest
and across all the 596 phenotypes. Notably, REGENIE suggested only including variants/gene
masks with MAC > 5 for association tests and set it in default for stable results. The MAC
was calculated for each phenotype respectively by REGENIE. Therefore, a large number of
rare variants were omitted due to low MAC and the exact number of tests omitted was
reported in the log files for each phenotype category. In addition, for implementation, we
ran REGENIE for all the variants in the original bfile but only included coding variants of
interest for analysis.
total were ignored due to low MAC as documented in the log file, which means 6,837,249
variants were ignored on average for each brain volume phenotype. Meanwhile, there were
130,349,763 results in total observed in the variant-level tests for these 101 brain volume
phenotypes and we focused on 31,096,939 results among them for coding variants of
interest. That is, 1,290,592 variants (including both coding variants of interest and other
variants) were present for each brain volume phenotype and among them 307890.5
variants were coding variants of interest on average. Our multiple testing adjustment would
use the number 31,096,939 here for these 101 brain volume phenotypes. The number of
coding variants of interest included in the variant-level tests for each of the 596 phenotypes
was retrieved by customized code for precise adjustment. Finally, the number of tests for all
phenotypes (for example, 31,096,939 for 101 brain volume phenotypes) was summed up
and this would yield 178,280,016 variant-trait tests in total as documented in Table S24. We
also included the total number of variant-level tests for each phenotype category Table S24,
which is helpful to track the number of variants.
We completely agree that this threshold is quite stringent, and we would like to use this
stringent threshold to ensure the reliability of our primary findings, given that we lack large-
scale independent dataset suitable for external replication analysis. For example, we used
the term ‘conservative’ to describe this P-value threshold in the manuscript (Page5, Line 24).
Following your suggestion, we have clarified these aspects of analysis in the revised
manuscript:
“The variant-level tests include all the coding variants of interest (n = 2,143,707) across all
596 phenotypes, but only those with sufficient MAC (MAC > 5) were tested and the MAC was
calculated for each phenotype respectively by REGENIE, so a large number of tests of
variants with MAC < 5 were ignored (Supplementary Note). The summary count and more
details are available in Table S24.” (Page 43, Lines 11-16)
“Consequently, this led us to use joint analysis with a stringent P-value cutoff, and an
internal validation procedure to assess the robustness of our findings” (Page 25, Lines 20-22)
“We note that our primary Bonferroni-type P-value threshold is quite stringent as the
phenotypes are not entirely independent, while we also...” (Page 43, Lines 20-21)
3. All the explored traits are of a quantitative nature. Especially with rare variants where
there may only be a hand full of carriers, outliers in these traits can drive the associations
and lead to inflated type 1 error (see
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4970685/). Have the authors considered any
mitigations for these cases? If not, it would be valuable to verify the identified
associations after applying inverse normal transformation (INT) of the quantitative data.
Response: Thank you so much for your insightful feedback and suggestions!
In terms of outliers, all the phenotype data present in our study were pre-processed to have
those entries with values greater than five times the median absolute deviation from the
median value removed. This step was part of our pipeline for generating phenotype data as
11
in our previous work. In the revised manuscript, we have included this information in the
Method and cited our previous work accordingly following your question:
“For each phenotype, values greater than five times the median absolute deviation from the
median value were removed as in our previous work1-4,10.” (Page 40, Lines 4-5)
Following your suggestions, we further verified our identified rare-variant associations by
applying rank-based inverse normal transformation (RINT). Specifically, we applied RINT by
calling “--apply-rint” in both step 1 and step 2 in REGENIE as suggested in their guidance
(https://rgcgithub.github.io/regenie/options/). We obtained all the summary statistics after
applying RINT for the previously identified associations that passed our primary threshold in
both variant-level tests and gene-level tests following the same pipeline. The new results
largely supported our original findings. Specifically, all associations except one (LPAR3 with
mean MD of uncinate fasciculus) still showed significance and passed the nominal threshold
adjusted for the number of signals undergoing RINT analysis at 4.7 × 10-4 (= 0.05/107) for
variant-level tests and 2.2 × 10-4 (= 0.05/224) for gene-based burden tests, respectively.
Using our original stringent threshold, 75.7% (81/107) variant-level associations still
survived our conservative threshold at 2.8 × 10-10, and the proportion became 85.0%
(91/107) under the suggestive threshold at 1 × 10-9. The proportion of gene-based
associations passing the primary threshold at 1 × 10-9 is 87.0% (195/224), and became 94.2%
(211/224) at a more lenient cutoff 1 × 10-8.
In the revised manuscript, we added two additional supplementary tables for the summary
statistics of RINT (Tables S22-S23) and discussed these results in the Discussion section and
provided the details in the Methods and Supplementary Note:
“There is also ongoing research regarding the best practice of performing rare variant
association tests. For example, Auer et al.127 pointed out that rare variant associations for
quantitative traits might be susceptible to outliers and non-normality and ignoring such
issues could result in false discoveries. Although outliers were removed in our pre-processing
steps for phenotype data (Methods), there is still potential concern about non-normality. We
verified all the identified associations by applying rank-based inverse normal transformation
(RINT) (Methods). The results largely supported our original findings (Tables S22-S23 and
Supplementary Note). Briefly, all associations except one (LPAR3 with the mean MD of
uncinate fasciculus) passed the nominal threshold adjusted for the number of signals
undergoing RINT analysis (4.7 × 10-4 = 0.05/107 for variant-level tests and 2.2 × 10-4 =
0.05/224 for gene-based burden tests, respectively). The majority of these associations also
remained significant under our primary stringent threshold.” (Page 23, Lines 25-32; Page 24,
Lines 1-4)
“To verify the robustness of the identified associations, rank-based inverse normal
transformation (RINT) was applied by calling ‘--apply-rint’ in both step 1 and step 2 of
REGENIE for all identified associations in our study, while we followed the same testing
procedure. The summary statistics produced after applying RINT were compared with the
original ones.” (Page 46, Lines 2-6)
12
4. For the validation analysis. I don’t think that the argument that the direction was
maintained in the larger cohort and that the p-values improve is a sufficiently strong one
(e.g., P6 Line 11). As outlined in the previous comment, outliers may be driving the
association and they may still be the driving force in the larger cohort. To make this a valid
argument, the authors should show that the p-value improved beyond what would be
expected from the increased sample size alone.
Response: Thank you so much for your comments! As mentioned in the response to your
Comment 3, we have considered the potential issues caused by outliers in our preprocessing
step for phenotype data and results from rank-based inverse normal transformation (RINT)
supported our findings. In internal replication, we compared the P-values from the discovery
sample and joint sample. For testing a null hypothesis of no effect, the summary statistics
from the joint sample are sufficient. For the purpose of confirming the associations by
internal replication based on sample splitting, we intended to investigate whether signals
derived from the discovery sample were attenuated in the enlarged sample (which might
indicate some evidence for false discovery). However, it is not direct to quantify the
confidence in this setting. If we assume that the effect sizes are constant, we could expect
that the Z-scores observed in the discovery sample (or the corresponding P-values) would
improve based on the enlarged sample at a scale of square root of the sample size.
Consistent with your comments, if the summary statistics (i.e. Z-scores and P-values)
observed in the joint sample have similar behaviors with the expected values, then such
associations would be reasonable. However, it is not direct to quantify the randomness in
this step, which led us to conduct a heuristic comparison between the analytical values and
observed values.
Following your suggestions, we calculated the expected Z-scores (and the corresponding P-
values) by multiplying the original Z-scores from the discovery sample by the square root of
the ratio of sample size of the joint sample and the discovery sample for each association.
We compared them with the observed Z-scores in the joint sample. Overall, they showed
agreement and similar behaviors were observed. Specifically, among the 50 associations
having smaller P-values in the joint sample, 34 of them have larger Z-scores than the
expected ones (or smaller P-values than the expected ones), while 40 of them have the
corresponding P-values at the same scale of the expected ones in terms of logarithm.
Notably, the potentially different effect sizes across stages, the instable estimates from rare
variants in the smaller sample, and the sampling randomness in the realization could still
complicate the interpretations here. In the revised manuscript, we have included them into
Table S4, and discussed them in the Supplementary Note:
“A comparison between the observed summary statistics in the internal analysis and the
expected improvements of these values in the enlarged joint sample is discussed in
Supplementary Note.” (Page 7, Lines 2-4)
5. The authors evaluate the variant hits in terms of existing GWAS hits. In particular for
DTI traits they uncover a rare variant in the VCAN gene. In an earlier GWAS (with
comparable sample size) an intronic SNP in the gene was strongly associated with DTI
traits (rs67827860 (P = 4.06 × 10−37; Elliot et al. ). What is the interpretation here given
13
the common variant shows a stronger association? Wouldn’t it be more likely that the rare
variants are only in LD with the variation causing driving the association?
Response: Thank you so much for raising this point! As noted, the common variant showed
a stronger association with DTI traits (has a smaller P-value) in a previous GWAS with
comparable sample size than two rare variants (rs2652098 and rs143368552) identified in
our study. Typically, common variants, which often rely on LD tagging, would have greater
statistical power as more carriers of such mutations are observed in the cohort. This fact can
partially explain why a smaller P-value was observed in the previous study when this
common variant alone was included in the test. Conversely, rare variants are expected to
capture more ‘direct’ effect and have independent signals that are potentially causal
compared with common variants in GWAS (for example, this point has been mentioned in
DeBoever et al. Nat Commu., PMID: 29691392, Wang et al. Nature, PMID: 34375979, and
has been observed in Backman et al. Nature, PMID: 34662886). However, the power might
be limited due the nature of rare variations as there are less carriers.
To clarify the relationships between these signals, we checked the LD and conducted
conditional analysis for DTI traits. We found both of these two rare variants are in low LD
with rs67827860 (R2 = 0.008 for both), calculated in the European ancestry from LDLink
(https://ldlink.nih.gov/?tab=home). This suggests that the rare variant is not simply tagging
the common variant.
Furthermore, we conducted conditional analysis by conditioning on this nearby common
variant in REGENIE (the conditional analysis is restricted to step 2 only; the genome-wide
predictors in step 1 were reused). Among 63 variant-level associations between these two
variants in VCAN and DTI traits (Table S2), 85.7% of these associations (54 out of 63)
survived the stringent threshold at 2.8 × 10-10, while all of these 63 associations remain
significant at a relaxed threshold 1 × 10-8 and have similar effect sizes.
Taken together, these results support the interpretation that two missense variants
identified in our study likely represent additional, independent associations around VCAN
locus in addition to the previously reported GWAS hit (or the causal variation in LD with
rs67827860). Following your suggestion, we have added the details of conditional analysis in
the method, discussed the results in the main text, and reported the summary statistics of
conditional analysis in an additional supplementary table Table S5:
“Notably, Elliot et al. identified an intronic variant rs67827860 with strong associations with
DTI traits. Thus, we conducted conditional analysis for all the 63 associations between these
two variants in VCAN and DTI traits by conditioning on this nearby common variant as a
covariate (Methods). We found that 85.7% of these associations still survived our stringent
threshold at 2.8 × 10-10 while all the associations passed our suggestive threshold at 1 × 10-8,
which supports the newly identified missense variants in VCAN as independent signals in
addition to the previously identified common variant (Table S5).” (Page 9, Lines 14-21)
“Conditional analysis was performed by specifying the nearby common variants as
covariates to assess the independence of the identified signals. The conditional analysis is
14
restricted to step 2 in REGENIE, while the genome-wide predictors in step 1 were reused.”
(Page 46, Lines 6-9)
6. When reading the manuscript it does not become quite clear which gene based burden
test the authors are using. There are multiple different ones implemented in regenie.
Please, can the authors provide detailed information (also in the results section on page 9
around line 20, not just the methods section).
Response: Thank you so much for your careful review! For all the gene-based tests in this
study, we used the burden test following the ‘max rule’ (default implementation in REGENIE,
see https://rgcgithub.github.io/regenie/options/#gene-based-testing). Specifically, the ‘max
rule’ scores each person based on the most damaging genotype they carry in terms of
dosage across the single variant sites of interest defined by annotation as a burden
mask/score, and then this burden score is tested for association similar to the manner of the
single variant test (also see https://rgcgithub.github.io/regenie/options/#gene-based-
testing). In the revised manuscript, these details are now provided in the main text as well
as Methods:
“In burden tests, the variants of interest defined by annotation and MAF (Methods) are
collapsed into a burden mask. Then, the burden score is calculated as the maximum
genotype dosage across the single variant sites in the mask, and this score is tested for
association (Methods).” (Page 10, Lines 22-25)
“Then for each given gene set, the score is calculated as the maximum of the genotype
dosage across all the variants in this set (the ‘max rule’ as the default implementation in
REGENIE), and the score is tested for association.” (Page 42, Lines 31-32; Page 43, Lines 1-2)
7. I recommend adding to the discussion also the authors’ perspective on the value of rare-
variant analyses. Compared to GWAS with the same sample size, much fewer loci-trait
associations have been identified. Does this mean that perhaps one should focus cost and
effort to other types of variation?
Response: Thank you so much for your suggestions! The fewer associations identified in our
study compared with GWAS partially result from the limited sample size and the nature of
rare mutations, though rare variants have stronger effect sizes. We also recognize that the
signals from rare variants and from common variants would provide complementary
information, which together contributes to a more complete human genetic landscape.
Following your recommendations, we have discussed the value of rare variant associations
in the Discussion section in the revised manuscript:
“Compared with GWAS of similar sample size (at the scale of 50,000) to our study, the
identified associations are much fewer partially due to the limited statistical power induced
by the low frequency of the protein-coding variants17,18,62. However, rare coding variants
offer more direct and stronger effects with interpretable biological implications, which would
contribute to complementary genetic information with common variants, prioritize the
effector genes, and elucidate the underlying mechanisms between gene-trait pairs.” (Page
26, Lines 5-11)
1. P4 Line 28: “whole body and shared genetic regulation across organs.” I think the
reasoning is a bit inconsistent in that the rare variants (which are limited to damaging,
protein altering variations) are viewed as regulators for processes across organs. Often
the focus on rare variation is to illuminate a more direct “mutation”-effect association
rather than uncovering a regulatory process. I recommend to reword this.
Response: Thank you so much for your thoughtful suggestions to improve the wording here!
We totally agree with this point as our study focuses on rare variants annotated as
predicted loss-of-function or damaging missense with interpretable biological consequences
at protein-level. In this revision, we have rephrased this sentence:
“whole body and shared genetic effects across organs.” (Page 4, Line 28)
We have also changed the wording in other places when suitable. The following are a few
examples:
“elucidate some shared genetic effects across organs.” (Page 3, Line 14)
“...provided additional evidence for its impact on heart structure and function.” (Page 10,
Line 5)
“Our novel discovery indicated that GEM may also impact the structural integrity of the
ascending aorta...” (Page 13, Lines 16-17)
“The consequences of these rare coding variants to human organs were largely
understudied.” (Page 22, Lines 25-26)
2. When reporting SNP effect sizes and association strengths it would be useful to have
the MAF or MAC in the main text
Response: Thank you so much for your helpful comments! Following your suggestion, we
went through our paper and added the MAF within the parentheses when reporting the
effect sizes (together with the information of P value and 95% CI) in the main text. The
following are a few examples:
“...we identified associations between spleen volume and two missense variants in
TNFRSF13B (rs72553883, MAF = 0.55%, effect = 0.025 L, effect = 0.37 s.d. units, 95% CI =
org
[0.29, 0.45], P = 5.6 × 10-19, and rs34557412, MAF = 0.66%, effect = 0.028 L, effect = 0.42
org
s.d. units, 95% CI = [0.34, 0.49], P = 2.0 × 10-28), ...” (Page 7, Lines 20-23)
“...the strongest association between PTEN and total brain volume with extraordinary effect
size when aggregating the pLoF and missense variants (MAF = 0.01%, effect = 386703.40
org
mm3, effect = 2.77 s.d. units, 95% CI = [2.22, 3.32], P = 5.8 × 10-23).” (Page 14, Lines 7-10)
16
“KCNA5 was associated with a regional peak circumferential strain measurement (MAF =
0.02%, effect = 5.11%, effect = 1.08 s.d. units, 95% CI = [0.63, 1.54], P = 3.2 × 10-6;
org
“Ecc_AHA_4”, Table S1) ...” (Page 17, Lines 27-29)
3. P8 Line 11-13: I do not think the reasoning/causality here is one to support the
association (i.e., the gene is associated with Schizophrenia (common) and that
Schizophrenia is associated with enlarged ventricles etc) to support the link between the
gene and brain volumes… Suggest rephrasing this.
Response: Thank you so much for pointing this out! We intended to point out fact that the
identified gene associated with both the brain volume and the mental disorder. In the
revised manuscript, we have simplified the wording and rephrased accordingly to avoid
potentially overclaiming the causal mechanism:
“ADRA1A was previously reported to be associated with schizophrenia43,44.” (Page 9, Lines 4-
5)
4. P38 Line 21 “Synonymous variants served as empirical null control to support the study-
wise P-value threshold for burden tests”. The statement is a bit vague and unclear. The
method behind this is only explained further down in the methods section. I recommend to
add a forward point to the relevant section to clarify that this will be explained below.
Response: Thank you so much for your thoughtful comments and suggestion on the writing!
Following your suggestion, we have added a forward point to the Method section in the
main text:
“Synonymous variants served as empirical null control to support the study-wise P-value
threshold for burden tests and the method would be detailed below in the section for
determining study-wise significance level.” (Page 41 Lines 23-25)
5. Regarding the Hardy-Weinberg filtering: I recommend to omit this step. Especially with
rare variants checking the HW may not be useful. Previous work that examined the HW QC
step suggested to retain variants and only examine the HW after associations have been
found:
https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.02.07.24301951v2
Response: Thank you so much for the suggestion and bringing our attention into this paper
(Greer et al.). Our sample size is around 50,000 and our HW filter was set at 1 × 10-15, which
would not remove too many variants as discussed in Greer et al. Specifically, in our previous
quality control (QC), only 8,272 variants were filtered out due to the HW QC step but passed
other QC steps. We carefully investigated the impact of these variants. Among these
variants, 2,202 variants were coding variants of interest based on our annotation method.
Then, we conducted the association tests for these new variants and reused the results from
step 1 of REGENIE. For variant-level associations, none of them were significant under the
suggestive P-value cutoff at 1 × 10-8. For gene-based burden test, 270 unique genes were
affected according to our definition for burden masks. When incorporating these variants
17
into the gene-based burden test, there is no new signals identified using the suggestive
threshold. In summary, the impact of the HW step in our QC has minimal impact on our
findings.
Following your suggestions, we mentioned this aspect of HW filtering in the Discussion
section and Supplementary Note:
“In addition, Greer et al.128 suggested retaining all the variants before conducting
association tests and examining the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium afterward to avoid the
over-removal of variants included in the study. We examined the variants filtered out by
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium step in our quality control step and no new discoveries were
identified, suggesting that this step had minimal impact on our study (Supplementary
Note).” (Page 24, Lines 4-10)
6. It appears as if genetics that influences blood flow affects the fMRI phenotypes. This
appears to be a bias in the analysis and interpretation of fMRI signals. Perhaps the
authors can comment on the need to incorporate cardiac features/genetics into the
analysis of fMRI data?
Response: Thank you so much for your comment! In the revised manuscript, we have
commented on this aspect of the analysis of fMRI data in the main text:
“Therefore, it might be helpful to integrate cardiac features and cardiac-related genetic
information when analyzing fMRI data, given that fMRI phenotypes are blood oxygen level-
dependent and are influenced by blood flow.” (Page 16, Lines 11-13)
18
